Paper Title:
Effective Regression Test Case Selection: A Systematic
Literature Review
Dataset: This is also a literature review paper, so it doesn't have its own numerical dataset. The authors collected and reviewed 47 empirical studies on regression test case selection, published between 2007 and 2015.
Preprocessing Method: The authors first built an assessment framework (covering four aspects: Test Problem, Test Model, System Under Test, and Dataset) to evaluate the empirical studies. They then followed Brereton et al.'s (2007) SLR guidelines, conducting the review in three stages -Planning, Conducting, and Documentation -to select papers, screen them, and extract data.
Model: No new AI/ML model was built here. Instead, the paper reviews various Regression Test Selection (RTS) techniques used across the 47 studies, including mining/learning-based methods, clustering, fuzzy logic, and particle swarm optimization.
Results: Among the 47 papers, 39% used mining/learning-based methods, while 65% were case studies based on small-size datasets — meaning large industrial-scale data was rarely used. Only 37% used publicly available datasets (making others hard to reproduce), and only 32% reported their limitations or threats to validity. Among the three effectiveness measures (cost, coverage, fault-detection), cost was the most commonly used (70%).
Contribution: This paper is one of the first to provide a structured evaluation framework for regression test case selection that jointly considers cost, coverage, and fault detection. Prior SLRs hadn't examined the relationship between these three factors together — this paper fills that gap and also outlines directions for future research.
Limitation: Most of the reviewed studies relied on small datasets and case studies, so it's uncertain how well the findings generalize to large industrial applications. Additionally, since there's no single standardized metric for measuring cost, coverage, or fault-detection, comparing results across different studies remains difficult.

Paper Title:
State of Practical Applicability of Regression Testing
Research: A Live Systematic Literature Review ***
Dataset: This is also a literature review, so there's no numerical dataset of its own. The authors searched five digital libraries (ACM, IEEE, Springer, Scopus, Wiley), initially finding 780 papers, then added 540 more through snowballing — totaling 1,320 candidate papers — which were screened down to 79 primary studies
Preprocessing Method: The authors first built search queries and ran them across the five databases. Two authors independently screened papers by title/abstract/keywords (achieving a Cohen Kappa agreement of 0.89, considered very high). They then performed forward and backward snowballing to find additional papers, and applied inclusion/exclusion criteria through full-text analysis to arrive at the final 79 papers. Finally, they validated their findings by surveying the authors of the selected studies (64% response rate) and 23 practitioners.
Model: No new model was built. Instead, the RT techniques used across the 79 papers were reviewed and categorized into four types: TCP (Test Case Prioritization), TCS (Test Case Selection), TSR (Test Suite Reduction), and TSA (Test Suite Augmentation).
Results: Among the 79 papers, TCP was by far the most researched technique, while TSR appeared in only 8 papers and TSA in just 1 -despite 60% of surveyed practitioners saying test maintenance/updating is a major real-world challenge. The author survey revealed that most techniques were never adopted in practice after publication (except in cases involving industry partnerships). The study identified 8 key challenges overall -including a mismatch in motivations, unrealistic experimentation, scalability issues, and a lack of academia-industry communication.
Contribution: The paper's biggest contribution is being the first "Live" Systematic Literature Review in regression testing — meaning they created an online repository that will be updated yearly with new papers, so the review won't become outdated. Beyond just reading papers, it also surveyed both the original authors and real-world practitioners directly, providing concrete evidence of the gap between academic research and practical adoption.
Limitation: The study's conclusions are limited to the 79 selected papers — findings could shift as new papers are published (though this is exactly why they maintain a live repository). Additionally, the practitioner survey used convenience sampling with only 23 respondents, which may not fully represent the industry and could introduce some selection bias.

Paper Title: Regression Testing of Web Service: A Systematic Mapping Study
Dataset: This is a systematic mapping study, so there's no numerical dataset. The authors searched 11 electronic databases (ACM, IEEE, Springer, ScienceDirect, etc.) for papers published between 2000–2013, starting with 3,244 papers, which were narrowed down through screening to 30 primary studies.
Preprocessing Method: Papers were filtered in stages: first removing "impurities" (irrelevant records), then applying exclusion criteria (C1, C2) to titles and abstracts, followed by duplicate removal across databases. A third criterion (C3) was then applied to the full text of remaining candidates. Papers from the same research line (i.e., updated/extended versions of the same work) were consolidated, keeping only the most representative version. An 8-item quality assessment checklist (Q1–Q8) was also used to evaluate each selected study, and a structured data extraction form was designed to collect information relevant to the research questions.
Model: No new model was built. Instead, the paper reviews and classifies existing regression testing techniques for web services into three main categories: Test Case Prioritization (TCP), Test Case Selection (TCS), and Test Suite Minimization (TSR) — plus one collaborative regression testing approach.
Results: Out of 30 primary studies, service integrators were the most studied stakeholder (76.7% of studies), since they have the least control over partner service evolution — making this the most challenging perspective. Among 7 identified challenges, cost and autonomy issues were the most researched, while test timing, dynamics, privacy, quota constraints, and concurrency remain understudied. A total of 48 prioritization techniques, 10 selection techniques, and only 2 minimization techniques were found. Most techniques focused on composite services (especially BPEL/orchestration-based) rather than choreography- or semantic-based services, and validation was generally done at small scale with limited real-world service data.
Contribution: This is claimed to be the first survey exclusively focused on web service regression testing (as opposed to broader web service testing surveys). It provides a comprehensive classification of stakeholders, challenges, standards, techniques, and validation methods used in this domain, and identifies concrete research gaps — such as underexplored challenges (privacy, dynamics, concurrency) and underrepresented service types (choreography-based, semantic-based).
Limitation: The authors acknowledge three main limitations: (1) potential bias in keyword selection during the search process, which could have caused relevant studies to be missed; (2) inaccuracy in data extraction due to insufficient detail in some primary studies (e.g., unclear validation methods or experimental settings); and (3) the specific choice of mapping-study methodology and classification schemes (borrowed from prior work) may have influenced the findings.

Application: A Survey****
Dataset: This is a survey paper, so there's no numerical dataset. The authors searched major repositories (IEEE Xplore, ACM Portal, ScienceDirect, Springer, Wiley, Google Scholar) covering 1988–2017, initially collecting more than 486 papers on regression testing, which were narrowed down to 79 papers specifically related to regression test case generation for software and web applications.
Preprocessing Method: Unlike the more formal SLRs in this collection, this paper doesn't follow a strict systematic protocol (no explicit research questions, Cohen Kappa agreement, or PRISMA-style screening). Papers were selected based on relevance to regression test case generation at the requirement, design, or coding level, and organized by their approach (e.g., UML-based, session-based, browser-based, model-based) and application to web applications.
Model: No new model was built. The paper reviews and categorizes existing test case generation techniques, including UML-based approaches (state diagrams, activity diagrams, sequence diagrams), session-based techniques, web browser interaction-based approaches, and web service-based approaches (e.g., using Control Flow Graphs).
Results: The survey found that very few approaches provide an actual usable tool for automated test case generation — most techniques remain theoretical or only partially validated. Techniques reviewed included session-based, browser-interaction-based, and workflow-based approaches, but most lacked large-scale experimental validation.

Paper Title: Software Testing Effort Estimation and Related Problems: A Systematic Literature Review
Dataset: This is also a literature review with no numerical dataset. Searching four databases (ACM, IEEE, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink) plus Google Search across three phases, the authors selected a total of 173 papers, of which only 84 directly addressed testing effort estimation, while the rest covered related topics.
Preprocessing Method: Following Kitchenham's SLR guidelines, the review was conducted in three separate phases (2016, 2018, 2019). Two search strings — "testing effort" and "testing estimation" — were used on the databases, and "testing effort estimation" was used for Google searches. Relevant papers were selected by screening thousands of results by title and abstract. Notably, the formal quality assessment step was done informally (based only on title/abstract relevance).
Model: No new predictive model was built. Existing testing effort estimation methods (such as TPA - Test Point Analysis, UCP - Use Case Points, and various machine learning/fuzzy logic-based approaches) were reviewed and classified according to seven criteria.
Results: Out of 173 selected papers, only 84 (48%) directly addressed testing effort estimation — demonstrating how limited direct research on this topic actually is. The most popular methods, TPA and UCP, are about 20 years old. Man-hours was the most commonly used effort measure, followed by man-days. While interest in this area has grown over the past decade, there remains a clear lack of reliable, industry-usable tools.
Contribution: The paper's biggest contribution is being the first study to place testing effort estimation within the broader context of all related software engineering topics. It provides concrete numerical evidence of just how large the research gap is in this specific area, and also identifies and critiques some existing solutions of questionable quality.
Limitation: The authors themselves acknowledge several limitations: a limited number of databases may have caused some important papers to be missed; in most cases, only abstracts/conclusions were analyzed rather than full texts; the review was conducted across three different time periods, which may affect consistency; and the entire data extraction process was done manually (without dedicated tools), increasing the risk of human error and making exact replication of the review difficult.

Paper Title: Test case prioritization methods: A systematic literature review
Dataset: This is a literature review with no numerical dataset of its own. Searching four databases (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, Springer) for papers published between 1999–2022, the authors initially found 393 papers, which were screened down to 68 primary studies (plus 4 manually added).
Preprocessing Method: The authors followed Kitchenham & Charters' PICOC framework to formulate research questions. Keywords and synonyms were analyzed to build Boolean search strings, followed by title/abstract screening, then inclusion/exclusion criteria (with inter-rater agreement validated at 87% between the two authors), and finally a 9-question quality assessment scoring system (studies scoring 3 or below were excluded) to arrive at the final set of papers.
Model: No new model was built. Existing TCP methods were reviewed and classified into 8 groups: source code coverage-based, human knowledge-based, cost-based, diagram-based, requirements-based, history-based, distribution-based, and hybrid methods.
Results: Among the 68 papers, source code coverage-based methods were the most common group (28%). The most striking finding was that not a single method was developed specifically for agile software development teams — terms like "agile," "scrum," and "kanban" did not appear in any of the 68 studies. It was also found that prioritized test execution consistently outperforms random/non-prioritized execution in terms of fault detection effectiveness and time savings.
Contribution: The paper's main contribution is creating a clear taxonomy and grouping of TCP methods across a broad time span (1999–2022), providing an in-depth analysis of each group, and most importantly, explicitly identifying the complete absence of TCP methods designed for agile contexts — a gap not clearly highlighted in prior SLRs. Unlike some existing SLRs limited to specific domains (e.g., model-based, requirements-based, or regression testing only), this review takes a more comprehensive, domain-agnostic approach.
Limitation: There is a risk of publication bias, since researchers tend to publish positive results more often than negative ones. Although the authors aimed for a recall of at least 85% (validated through a pilot Google Scholar search), there remains a risk of missing relevant studies. The authors also acknowledge that the data extraction process involved some subjective judgment and carries a risk of missing important data.

Paper Title: Test case prioritization based on fault sensitivity analysis using ranked NSGA-2
Dataset: A custom Java project ("Project P") was used (5 modules, 7 classes) to illustrate the methodology, and three open-source Java projects from the SIR (Software-artifact Infrastructure Repository) — Ant, Jmeter, and Jtopas — were used for the main experiments. Additionally, 5 variants of Project P (P1–P5) were created.
Preprocessing Method: First, fault seeding and mutation techniques were used to artificially inject faults for testing purposes. Test cases were then generated for each project (at both class and method levels). Software metrics were extracted, producing 5 data files (TestCases_Faults.csv, TestCases_Classes.csv, Class_Weights.csv, TestCases_Weights.csv, TestCases.csv), where object-oriented metrics such as McCabe's Cyclomatic Complexity, CBO, and LCOM were used for outlier detection and weight calculation.
Model: The main model proposed in this paper is NSGA-2 (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II) — a multi-objective genetic algorithm that simultaneously optimizes three fitness functions (APFD, Sensitivity Index, and Cost) to prioritize test cases. The initial population size equals the number of test cases, iterations are set to twice the number of test cases, with a crossover rate of 0.5 and mutation rate of 0.25.
Results: NSGA-2 achieved the highest APFD scores across all datasets (P1–P5, Ant, Jmeter, Jtopas) — outperforming Greedy, 2-Opt, GA, Honey Bee Optimization, African Buffalo Optimization, and AHP-based methods (e.g., 98.14% on P5). The Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test confirmed these differences were statistically significant (p<0.05). The three-point analysis showed that removing APFD as an objective caused the worst performance degradation, while keeping Cost or SI alongside APFD helped avoid the local-optimum trap that single-objective approaches often fall into.
Contribution: The paper's main contribution is proposing a novel metric called the Sensitivity Index (SI), which combines code complexity (at the class level) with test case history (at the test level) to identify fault-prone areas. It also applies a ranked NSGA-2 to jointly optimize APFD, SI, and Cost as a multi-objective problem, outperforming existing single-objective approaches and other multi-objective methods (such as MOBF).
Limitation: The paper itself acknowledges that treating SI and APFD as separate objectives can result in multiple different APFD values for the same SI value, since a test case covering a "target point" doesn't always guarantee it will detect a fault. Additionally, experiments were conducted mainly on small-to-medium-sized Java projects (Project P, Ant, Jmeter, Jtopas), so scalability to large industrial systems remains unverified. The authors themselves note that future work should focus on integrating SI and APFD into a single unified objective for better control over prioritization.

Paper Title: Test Case Prioritization Using Dragon Boat Optimization for Software Quality Testing
Dataset: Four standard benchmark datasets were used: GZIP, GREP, TCAS, and CS-TCAS. These are widely used standard programs/datasets in regression testing and test case prioritization research.
Preprocessing Method: The test case prioritization problem was formulated as a mapping problem, where a fitness value (f) is calculated for each test case based on APFD and APTC. Effective Execution Time (EET) was calculated to determine how long each test case takes to reach maximum statement coverage. The DBOA algorithm was then applied by initializing a population (population size = number of test cases), evaluating the fitness of each agent (dragon boat), and iteratively optimizing.
Model: The main proposed model is TCP-DBOA (Test Case Prioritization using Dragon Boat Optimization Algorithm) — a metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by dragon boat racing, which determines test case ordering using mathematical factors such as social behavior factor, acceleration factor, attenuation factor, and imbalance rate. Parameter settings: learning rate 0.01, ReLU activation, 50 epochs, dropout 0.5, batch size 5.
Results: TCP-DBOA achieved the best results across all four datasets — outperforming MHHO-TCP, Firefly Algorithm (FA), PSD, LBS, and Greedy methods in terms of APFD (e.g., 97.17–97.24% on GZIP versus only 92–94% for Greedy). It also achieved the lowest Average Time Execution (ATE) and Computational Time (CT), demonstrating both speed and efficiency.
Contribution: The paper's main contribution is being the first to apply the Dragon Boat Optimization Algorithm to test case prioritization — a relatively new metaheuristic method (proposed in 2023). It introduces a novel approach that leverages social psychology-based team dynamics (social loafing, social incentive) for optimization, effectively handling large search spaces and balancing exploration-exploitation, outperforming existing GA, HHO, and PSO-based methods.
Limitation: The author acknowledges that the approach is limited to a specific set of benchmark datasets (GZIP, GREP, TCAS, CS-TCAS), which may not fully represent the diversity of real-world testing environments. Scalability to massive, more complex datasets remains unaddressed, and the model does not incorporate dynamic software changes or real-time adaptability — limiting its applicability in agile or continuously evolving development processes. Additionally, the impact of environmental factors such as hardware discrepancies or network conditions on TCP was not explored.

Paper Title: A Collaborative Filtering Recommender System for Test Case Prioritization in Web Applications
Dataset: The study uses test cases and their historical test execution information from web applications. This historical information is used to identify execution behavior and testing-related relationships among test cases
Preprocessing Method: The historical test execution data is organized into a representation suitable for collaborative filtering. Testing history is used to identify similarities or relationships among test cases based on their previous execution behavior.
Model: The main model is a Collaborative Filtering-based Recommender System. It applies the collaborative filtering concept from recommender systems to identify relationships among test cases and recommend which test cases should be executed earlier.
Results: The experimental evaluation shows that the proposed collaborative filtering approach is effective for test case prioritization and can provide competitive performance compared with existing test case prioritization techniques. Historical testing information helps generate an effective test execution order for earlier fault detection.
Contribution: The main contribution is the application of collaborative filtering from recommender systems to test case prioritization. The study proposes a recommendation-based prioritization approach for web application regression testing and introduces a new perspective for prioritizing test cases using historical test execution information.

In CPM, 2-way was about 30% faster than the worst technique, while in Masplas it was about 40% faster. The oracle comparators could introduce false positives or negatives, and execution times were approximated rather than measured for individual test cases. Then the resulting test cases are ordered using three HTTP-request-based criteria: (1) the number/frequency of common HTTP requests in pages, (2) the ordered length of HTTP-request chains, and (3) the order dependency between HTTP requests. Dataset: The study does not use a conventional dataset. Instead, it evaluates the prioritization algorithms on five dynamic JSP-based web applications, with 16 modified versions of each website. They then manually injected faults at random locations and generated corresponding test cases using Selenium IDE's capture-and-replay functionality. A test-case-versus-fault matrix, test-case execution-time matrix, and fault-severity matrix were constructed. Fault severity was determined using a survey of 20 IT professionals with at least five years of relevant experience, while execution times were obtained using Selenium and Emma.

For dynamic prioritization, DGFP and DCFP were never worse than their static counterparts, while DLFP repeatedly performed worse. Contribution: The paper introduces the use of execution frequency of modified code as a test-prioritization criterion. Paper Title: A safe, efficient regression test selection technique
Dataset: The study used two sets of C programs. Study 1 used seven Siemens programs (138–512 lines, 8–21 procedures each) with 132 faulty versions and test pools of 1,054–5,542 tests, where each version contained seeded faults. Study 2 used the player subsystem from the Empire game (49,316 lines, 766 functions) with five real modified versions and a constructed functional test suite of 1,035 tests based on command documentation
Preprocessing Method: The technique constructs control flow graphs (CFGs) for the original and modified program, then synchronously traverses both graphs to identify edges where code differs. Tests that traversed those changed edges are selected using pre-collected test history (edge traces). Both intraprocedural (SelectTests) and interprocedural (SelectInterTests) algorithms are presented, with the latter handling procedure calls recursively and avoiding redundant analysis
Model: The paper does not propose any machine learning or statistical model. It presents a deterministic, rule-based regression test selection algorithm with formal proofs of safety (selects all fault-revealing tests) under controlled regression testing conditions, and analyzes its complexity, precision, and efficiency analytically
Results: Empirical results showed that interprocedural test selection reduced test suite size by an average of 44.4% for the Siemens programs (saving up to 53% of total time) and over 95% for the player program (saving 82–93% of testing time). Analysis costs were negligible (under 22 seconds for Siemens, estimated under 25 minutes for player). The safe technique always detected faults when fault-revealing tests existed, unlike minimization techniques which had very low fault detection probability
Contribution: The paper presents the first regression test selection technique that is provably safe (selects all fault-revealing tests) under controlled regression testing, while being more precise than other safe techniques. It handles all language constructs and modification types, supports both intraprocedural and interprocedural selection, and is fully automatable with efficient O(|T|·min(n,n′)) expected runtime, implemented in the DejaVu tool
Limitation: Threats include small subject programs (Siemens) with seeded rather than real faults, constructed test suites for player (no existing suites), limited generalizability to other languages and larger systems, and the algorithm is only safe under controlled regression testing conditions (deterministic execution, non-obsolete tests, correct outputs on original). The interprocedural analysis for player required estimation due to tool limitations

Techniques: A Systematic Review
Dataset: The systematic review analyzed 2,923 papers from seven major databases (Inspec, Compendex, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Springer LNCS, Web of Science) published up to 2006. Results: The review identified 32 distinct regression test selection techniques, with 18 appearing in only one study each. Paper Title: Hybrid Regression Test Selection
Dataset: The study used 32 open-source Java Maven projects from GitHub, totaling 2,707 revisions and over 124 million lines of code. Projects ranged from small (e.g., invokebind with 23 tests) to large (e.g., closure-compiler with 11,309 tests), and were categorized as short-running (test execution <60s) or long-running (>60s) based on their test suite execution time
Preprocessing Method: The proposed HyRTS technique combines method-level and file-level RTS analysis. It computes method-level changes only for files with fine-grained method modifications (e.g., method body changes), while using fast file-level checksums for file additions, deletions, or header changes. Test dependencies are collected dynamically via bytecode instrumentation using ASM, and the selected tests are those whose dependencies overlap with the computed hybrid changes
Model: The paper does not propose a machine learning or statistical model. It presents a deterministic, rule-based hybrid RTS algorithm that applies change transformations (basic and aggressive) to combine RTS at multiple granularities. Formal proof of safety is provided, showing that hybrid RTS via change transformation cannot introduce new safety issues compared to traditional safe RTS techniques
Results: HyRTS selected 18.35% of tests on average versus 27.18% for file-level RTS (8.83 percentage points more precise), and was 21.1% faster in offline testing time (31.60s vs. 40.06s). However, online performance was less consistent due to costly method-level dependency collection. The HyRTS_F variant (transforming instance method additions/deletions to file-level changes) consistently outperformed file-level RTS in both offline and online modes, while HyRTS_B (adding basic-block analysis) was not cost-effective
Contribution: This is the first hybrid RTS approach that combines multiple granularities (file and method levels) to leverage the precision of fine-grained RTS and the low overhead of coarse-grained RTS. The paper provides extensive empirical evidence on 124M LoC, a detailed study of each method-level change type's impact, and introduces HyRTS_F as a superior variant. The implementation is publicly available as a Maven plugin
Limitation: Threats include external validity (subjects are open-source Java Maven projects, may not generalize to other languages, build systems, or proprietary systems), construct validity (metrics may not capture all cost-benefit trade-offs), and the fact that HyRTS can be slower than FRTS in online mode for some projects due to expensive method-level dependency collection. The study also only compares against file-level RTS, not method-level RTS, as prior work already showed method-level RTS is slower

Paper Title: Regression test selection for Java softwar
Dataset: The study used four Java subjects: SIENA (event notification system, 185 methods, 7 versions, 138 tests), JEdit (text editor, 3,495 methods, 11 versions, 189 tests), JMeter (web testing tool, 109 methods, 5 versions, 50 tests), and RegExp (regex library, 168 methods, 10 versions, 66 tests). Test suites provided 46–75% method coverage
Preprocessing Method: The technique constructs Java Interclass Graphs (JIGs) representing control flow, type information, inheritance, polymorphism, exception handling, and external library interactions. A graph-traversal algorithm compares original and modified JIGs to identify dangerous edges, then selects test cases whose coverage overlaps these edges using a coverage matrix from program instrumentation.
Model: No machine learning model is proposed. The paper presents a deterministic, safe regression test selection algorithm with formal safety proof under assumptions (no reflection, deterministic execution, independent external classes). It uses class hierarchy analysis for call resolution and supports both edge-level and method-level instrumentation granularitie
Results: Test suite reduction varied widely across subjects and versions: SIENA selected 2–90% of tests, JEdit 15–90%, JMeter 10–95%, RegExp 25–80%. The technique was effective but reduction depended on change location and program structure. Edge-level selection could further reduce test suites beyond method-level in 49% of cases, with significant differences for some SIENA versions

More precise than prior C++ and firewall-based approaches. The RETEST system implements the technique and empirical results show significant test suite reduction is achievable
Limitation: Current profiler (JVMPI-based) cannot record individual statement coverage, causing imprecision (method-level instead of edge-level). Assumptions limit applicability (no reflection, deterministic execution, independent external libraries). Empirical subjects are relatively small and may not generalize to larger industrial systems. Edge-level instrumentation not fully implemented due to profiler limitations

Paper Title:
A Comparative Study of Coarse- and Fine-
Grained Safe Regression Test-Selection
Techniques
Dataset: The study used three subject groups: seven Siemens programs (100–516 lines, 7–41 versions each, with 1,000 branch-adequate test suites per program), the space program (6,218 executable lines, 38 versions, 1,000 test suites), and the player subsystem from Empire (49,316 lines, 5 real modified versions, one test suite of 1,033 test cases)
Preprocessing Method: Two safe RTS tools were compared: DejaVu (fine-grained, statement/CFG-level) and TestTube (coarse-grained, function/global variable-level). Both collect test dependencies on the original version, compute changes between versions, and select tests whose dependencies overlap with changes. TestTube uses checksums on coarse entities, while DejaVu performs simultaneous CFG traversal to identify dangerous edges.
Model: No machine learning model is proposed. The paper presents a comparative empirical study of two deterministic safe RTS algorithms, using a cost model (analysis time + execution time) to evaluate cost-effectiveness. A hybrid approach combining TestTube's coarse analysis followed by DejaVu's fine analysis on truncated code is also explored.
Results: On Siemens programs, both tools reduced test suites but analysis costs exceeded retest-all; DejaVu was more precise but more expensive than TestTube. On space, TestTube nearly matched DejaVu's precision with lower cost, but both were less efficient than retest-all. On player, DejaVu saved 82–93% of testing time; TestTube matched DejaVu on 3 versions but selected all tests on 2 versions. The hybrid approach on space outperformed both individual tools
Contribution: First comprehensive comparative empirical study of two safe RTS techniques (DejaVu vs. TestTube) measuring both precision and efficiency with actual execution costs. Demonstrates trade-offs between coarse-grained (cheaper but less precise) and fine-grained (more precise but costlier) analysis, and introduces and evaluates a hybrid approach that combines both for better cost-effectiveness.
Limitation: hreats include small subject programs (Siemens) with seeded faults limiting generalizability; DejaVu simulation on player due to instrumentation limitations; coarse cost model ignoring human effort and other costs; and results may not generalize to other languages, environments, or larger industrial systems. The hybrid prototype required a non-production interface (Hybrid.java) that would not exist in a real implementation

Paper Title:
Systematic Literature Review on Regression Test Prioritization
Techniques
Dataset: The systematic review analyzed 65 primary studies (50 experiments and 15 case studies) published up to February 2011, identified from six databases (Inspec, ACM, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Springer LNCS, Google Scholar). These studies reported 106 regression test prioritization (RTP) techniques, with artifacts primarily from the Software Infrastructure Repository (SIR), including Siemens programs, Space, and various Java subjects
Preprocessing Method: The review followed Kitchenham's systematic literature review guidelines, with a three-stage selection process (title, abstract, full-text screening) by multiple researchers. Techniques were classified into eight categories: coverage-based, modification-based, fault-based, requirement-based, history-based, genetic-based, composite, and other approaches
Model: No predictive model is proposed. The paper is a systematic literature review that synthesizes existing RTP techniques and their empirical evidence. It performs qualitative analysis comparing techniques by approach, granularity (17 levels identified), input method, language dependency, artifacts, tools, and metrics, without proposing any new prioritization algorithm
Results: Coverage-based approaches dominated (44% of techniques), followed by composite (18%) and fault-based (11%). Source code was the primary input (58%), and 50% of techniques were language-independent. APFD (Average Percentage of Faults Detected) was the most used metric (29 studies). Additional (feedback-based) techniques consistently outperformed total techniques in fault detection. Statement-level techniques were better than function-level for C, but granularity had no effect for Java

Limitation: Threats include exclusion of non-English papers, potential missed studies due to database search limitations, inability to perform statistical aggregation due to heterogeneous reporting (specific APFD values often missing), and the review only covers papers up to February 2011. Paper Title: Enhancing Automated Unit Test Generation with Large Language Models: A Systematic Literature Review
Dataset: he surveyed studies rely on large-scale datasets, most notably Methods2Test (780,944 focal method-test pairs from GitHub), UniTSyn (a multi-lingual dataset of 2.7 million focal-test pairs across five languages), and Atlas (2.5 million focal-assert pairs). However, the paper highlights that these datasets are primarily Java/Python-focused, often noisy, and lack multi-level alignment (method, class, project, and requirement levels) or reasoning process documentation, which limits model generalizability and test quality
Preprocessing Method: The typical processing pipeline for LLM-based test generation starts by providing the target function, class, or project under test (augmented with documentation, comments, or usage examples) to the LLM. The model then generates candidate unit tests consisting of input values, execution logic, and test oracles. These generated tests are iteratively refined through feedback loops—using compilation or execution results (coverage, failures, error logs)—to repair, augment, or optimize the tests until they become executable, high-coverage, and bug-revealing
Model: The field is dominated by decoder-only LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5, GPT-4, CodeLlama, and StarCoder), accounting for 88.28% of usage. The primary adaptation strategies are: (1) Prompt engineering (79% of studies) using zero/few-shot, chain-of-thought, and retrieval-augmented generation; (2) Fine-tuning (21%) with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA and domain adaptation; and (3) Agent-based methods (6%) where specialized autonomous agents handle generation, execution, and repair collaboratively
Results: The review finds that LLM-based methods substantially outperform traditional tools (like EvoSuite and Pynguin) in semantic reasoning, readability, and bug detection, with hybrid frameworks achieving 9–10% average coverage improvements and up to 5× correctness boosts. However, vanilla LLM prompting without structural constraints still underperforms traditional tools in compilation success and structural coverage, showing that LLMs alone are not yet a full replacement but excel when augmented with program analysis and repair mechanisms
Contribution: This paper provides the first comprehensive, task-oriented systematic literature review of LLM-based unit test generation, synthesizing 116 primary studies (2021–2025). It maps the full task landscape (test generation, input generation, oracle generation, and test evolution), categorizes LLM adaptation strategies (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and agent-based approaches), analyzes evaluation practices, and identifies key empirical challenges with evidence-based solutions—offering a consolidated foundation for future research
Limitation: Current LLM-based approaches are heavily concentrated on test generation (84 studies) while input generation (5 studies), oracle construction (18 studies), and test evolution (13 studies) remain underexplored. The review also notes heavy reliance on Java/Python benchmarks (e.g., Defects4J, HumanEval) with scarce coverage for Rust, Go, or Kotlin; persistent issues with hallucinated assertions, invalid syntax, and non-deterministic outputs; and a lack of standardized evaluation frameworks, with 26% of studies still non-replicable due to missing artifacts.

Paper Title: Selective regression testing for web applications created with google web toolkit
Dataset: The paper evaluates the technique on two GWT-based applications: StockWatcher (a small tutorial app with 11 modified versions and 12 web tests) and Hupa (a large real-world mail client with ~40,000 lines of code across 484 classes, using 4 modified versions and 26 acceptance tests)
Preprocessing Method: The pipeline involves: (1) instrumenting web tests to collect code identifiers (CIDs) from the original version; (2) comparing Java source code ASTs of old and new versions using Extended Java Interclass Graphs (EJIGs) to detect changes; (3) selecting only those web tests whose logged CIDs cover modified code for rerun; and (4) linking selected tests back to specific code changes to aid debugging
Model: The core technique is a static regression test selection algorithm adapted from Harrold et al., which uses AST-based EJIGs to compare two program versions in parallel and detect "dangerous edges" (changes). It introduces deterministic CIDs for every AST node, injects them into generated JavaScript via a modified GWT compiler, and maps execution traces back to Java code to identify affected tests
Results: For StockWatcher, the tool selected 89% of tests (safely including all expected ones) with only 9% unnecessary selections. For Hupa, it selected 37% against an expected 33%, with change categorization precision between 78–100%. The tool completed analysis in ~90 seconds, roughly half the time of running the full test suite
Contribution: This is the first selective regression testing technique for GWT-based web applications. It bridges the Java-to-JavaScript gap using CIDs traced through the GWT compiler, detects and categorizes code changes down to expression level, and links selected web tests back to specific Java modifications, enabling efficient fault localization without manual JavaScript tracing.
Limitation: The technique does not support JSNI native methods, UIBinder layout changes (HTML/XML), broken hyperlinks, or fully guaranteed controlled regression testing due to asynchronous client-server interactions. Additionally, incomplete CID injection for every expression leads to some unnecessary test selections

Paper Title: Performance regression testing target prioritization via performance risk analysis
Dataset: The study uses 100 real-world performance regression issues randomly sampled from three large open-source projects: MySQL (50 issues), PostgreSQL (25), and Chrome (25). For evaluation on new commits, 600 randomly selected recent commits from six software systems (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Apache, Squid, GCC, V8) are used, with performance benchmarking to establish ground truth for regression detection.
Preprocessing Method: The approach first parses code commits and maps changes to program constructs (functions, loops, basic blocks). It then performs static cost modeling to estimate expensiveness of changed operations and frequency estimation to determine if changes lie in hot paths (loops, recursive functions, frequently called functions). These two factors are combined using a risk matrix to assign risk levels (extreme/high/moderate/low), which are aggregated into a risk score. Testing targets are then prioritized based on this risk score
Model: The core technique is Performance Risk Analysis (PRA)—a lightweight static analysis that estimates a commit's risk of introducing performance regression. It uses: (1) a cost model with abstract cost units (δ) for different operations, (2) frequency estimation via loop trip counts and call path analysis, and (3) a risk matrix combining expensiveness and frequency. An optional extension (PRA-Slicing) performs forward program slicing to detect indirect performance impacts through data/control flow propagation
Results: PRA successfully alarms 92% of the 100 studied problematic commits. On 600 new commits, PRA recommends only 14–22% of commits for testing while still covering 87–95% of all risky commits. PRA-Slicing achieves higher coverage (95%) but lower reduction (78%). The approach saves significant testing time—for GCC, up to two months of testing cost. PerfScope runs in under 2 minutes (PRA) or 6 minutes (PRA-Slicing) per commit analysis
Contribution: First white-box approach for performance regression testing target prioritization via code change risk analysis. Provides an empirical study of 100 real-world performance regression issues, revealing that problematic changes commonly involve expensive operations in hot paths or indirect effects via data/control flow. Implements and open-sources PerfScope tool. Demonstrates that analyzing just 14–22% of commits can catch 87–95% of performance regressions, significantly improving testing efficiency.
Limitation: Limited to C/C++ code (LLVM/Clang), not supporting other languages. Cost model focuses on computation, with limited modeling for I/O, networking, or OS kernel behavior. Does not handle sophisticated issues like resource contention or caching effects. PRA-Slicing can be imprecise and expensive for deep analysis. Chrome could not be evaluated due to compilation challenges. Performance regression judgment thresholds are subjective and require tuning per project. The study focuses on repeatable regressions, not performance bugs

Paper Title: A Slice-Based Change Impact Analysis for Regression Test Case Prioritization of Object-Oriented Programs
Dataset: The study evaluated the approach on 15 Java programs: 10 benchmark programs from the Software-artifact Infrastructure Repository (SIR) and 5 academic assignment programs. The programs ranged from 54 to 7,646 LOC, with 296 total test cases. Mutation faults were generated using MuClipse, with 514 mutants used across the 15 programs.
Preprocessing Method: The Java programs were converted into an intermediate representation and analyzed to identify data, control, and object-oriented dependencies. Hierarchical decomposition slicing was then used to identify the program parts affected by a change. Test coverage was obtained using JaBUTi, and test cases with more than 50% coverage were considered before selecting those relevant to the affected program parts.
Model: The paper proposed a static, coupling-based test case prioritization approach called H-PTCACC/FPANC. It constructs an Affected Slice Graph (ASG), calculates the Affected Component Coupling (ACC) of affected nodes to estimate their fault-proneness, groups the nodes using K-means clustering, assigns weights to the groups, and prioritizes test cases based on the fault-prone affected nodes they cover.
Results: The prioritized test cases killed approximately 70%–95% of the generated mutants across the programs, with an average of about 84%. The proposed FPANC approach achieved 80.6% affected-node coverage compared with 77.2% for the compared ANC approach and achieved approximately an 8% improvement in APFD.
Contribution: The paper introduced a change-impact-based prioritization technique for object-oriented programs that considers not only which program parts are affected by a change, but also how fault-prone those affected parts are. By using affected component coupling to estimate fault-proneness, the approach gives higher priority to test cases that cover more critical affected nodes.

Paper Title:
A Hybrid Approach to Software Testing Efficiency Stacked Ensembles and Deep
Q-Learning for Test Case Prioritization and Ranking
Dataset: The study uses a year-long benchmark testing dataset containing 89 individual test cases, 25,594 test executions, and 352 CI cycles, with each cycle containing at least six test cases. The experiments refer to this as the Paint-Control dataset and use the historical execution data for both prioritization and ranking.

They create features such as Gap in Run Time, Gap Cats, Same Cycle Run, cycle_Run, Last Run, Failure Percentage, and Test Case Maturity. After testing more than 50 combinations of test-maturity features using mutual information, they select the most informative attributes. For the final classification, six main features—my_maturity, last_run, Cycle, failure_percentage, Month, and times_ran—are selected.

For test-case prioritization, Random Forest, Bayesian Network, SVM, and Gradient Boosted models are evaluated, followed by voting-based ensembles. The best prioritization model is the Random Forest/selected ensemble approach. For ranking within priority levels, a Deep Q-Network (DQN) is evaluated using Listwise, Pairwise Rank, and Pairwise Verdict environments. Among the individual classifiers, Gradient Boosted achieved 0.9716 accuracy and Random Forest 0.9664; however, the selected three-model ensemble achieved 0.9836 accuracy with only 8.9017 s computation time, compared with 0.8265 and 26.3217 s for the four-model ensemble. With 1,000 test cases, Pairwise Rank reached a reported NRPA of 0.9989902373076025. Genetic operators produced only modest metric improvements in several cases, while increasing runtime by approximately 339%, 680%, and up to 850% compared with the base RL agents.
Contribution: The paper proposes a hybrid AI-based framework that separates test-case prioritization from test-case ranking and applies different learning techniques to each task. It combines feature-engineered supervised ML for assigning priority groups with Deep Q-Learning for adaptive ranking and explores Genetic Algorithms as an additional optimization layer. Paper Title: BugPrioritizeAI for multimodal test case prioritisation using bug reports, code changes, and test metadata
Dataset: The study uses two real-world Java software-testing datasets: Defects4J and BugSwarm. Defects4J contains reproducible faults from 17 Java open-source projects, together with buggy/fixed versions, test cases, fault information, and code changes. BugSwarm contains failed and fixed CI builds from more than 1,000 open-source GitHub projects; the authors retain only its Java-based projects to maintain a homogeneous environment with Defects4J. The datasets provide bug reports/bug information, commit and code-change data, test execution logs, and fault-revealing test outcomes.
Preprocessing Method: Bug reports were cleaned using regular expressions to remove HTML tags, stack traces, and other noise, then tokenized and converted into semantic embeddings using BERT. Code changes were parsed with GitPython to extract features such as lines added/deleted, modified files, and change entropy. Test metadata was obtained from test logs and JaCoCo coverage reports, including historical failures, coverage, and execution-related information. The researchers then created bug–commit–test triples, filtered unreliable/ambiguous mappings, and linked bug reports to tests using cosine similarity and code changes to tests using file/function coverage overlap. Numerical feature vectors were standardized/normalized, and missing change features could be imputed with median statistics and flagged.
Model: The proposed BugPrioritizeAI framework uses BugTestRankNet as its core neural ranking model. Bug reports, code changes, and test metadata are processed through separate encoders and projected into a common latent space. An attention-based fusion mechanism learns how much weight to give each modality before producing a scalar priority score for every test case. The model is trained using Binary Cross-Entropy loss with Adam optimization, dropout, weight decay, and early stopping. The resulting scores are sorted in descending order to produce the test execution order. SHAP is additionally used to explain why individual tests receive high or low priority.
Results: BugPrioritizeAI achieved the best overall performance among the evaluated methods, obtaining 84.3% APFD, 4.8 TTFF, and 42.7 s TET. This was higher than DeepTCP (77.9% APFD, 7.2 TTFF, 65.3 s TET), RiskMiner (74.5%, 8.4, 72.1 s), History-Based (68.8%, 10.7, 85.4 s), Coverage-Based (65.3%, 13.2, 98.7 s), and Random (52.1%, 17.6, 120.5 s). In the project-wise evaluation, BugPrioritizeAI improved APFD over DeepTCP by approximately 5–8 percentage points across the reported Chart, Lang, Math, Closure, and Mockito projects while also reducing TTFF. In cross-dataset testing, training on Defects4J and testing on BugSwarm produced 81.2 APFD vs. 72.6 for DeepTCP, while training on BugSwarm and testing on Defects4J produced 83.7 vs. 75.8 APFD. The ablation study also showed that combining all three modalities produced 0.82 APFD on Defects4J and 0.79 on BugSwarm, compared with 0.71/0.68 using bug reports only, 0.73/0.69 using code changes only, and 0.75/0.73 using test metadata only. Removing a modality reduced APFD by roughly 4–11%, supporting the benefit of multimodal fusion.
Contribution: The paper introduces an explainable multimodal test case prioritization framework that jointly learns from three previously separated sources of evidence: bug-report semantics, source-code changes, and historical test metadata. Its main contribution is the BugTestRankNet architecture with attention-based fusion, which learns cross-modal relationships instead of treating each information source independently. The framework also integrates SHAP-based explanations and an optional developer feedback loop, making the prioritization decisions more interpretable and potentially more useful in CI/CD environments. The evaluation additionally examines cross-dataset generalization using Defects4J and BugSwarm.
Limitation: The framework depends heavily on the quality and completeness of bug reports, code-change information, coverage data, dependency links, and test metadata. Noisy or duplicated bug reports, missing coverage/flakiness information, or outdated dependency data can weaken the learned ranking. The evaluation is limited to public, Java-based datasets, so performance on enterprise-scale, proprietary, or polyglot industrial systems remains uncertain. The current framework is also primarily batch-based rather than real-time, so it cannot continuously adapt to incoming CI/CD changes without retraining. Hyperparameter tuning was performed on a relatively small validation set, and the practical usefulness of SHAP explanations has not yet been evaluated through a structured developer study. Finally, APFD, TTFF, and TET do not capture every practical consideration, such as developer effort or fault severity.

Paper Title: pytest-ranking: A Regression Test Prioritization Tool for Python
Dataset: The evaluation uses 718 selected commits/builds from 14 open-source Python projects, producing 4,308 actual test-suite runs (TSRs)—six test orders for each selected build. The projects were selected from popular PyPI projects that use Pytest and GitHub Actions. Initially, the researchers collected 27,224 builds containing TSRs, but selected a smaller subset for actual rerunning because of computational cost. The final dataset contained 1,121 TSRs with test failures, 720 with at least one regression failure, and 660 with only regression failures.
Preprocessing Method: The researchers filtered projects and CI builds based on metadata, GitHub Actions usage, Python/Pytest compatibility, build status, and test-suite duration. For each historical build, they restored the repository to the build's original commit and controlled dependency versions using UV's --exclude-newer option to avoid failures caused by installing newer dependencies. During execution, the tool collected test duration and outcomes and stored the information in the Pytest cache. The prioritization scores from QTF, RecentFail, and SimChgPath were normalized to [0,1] before being combined.
Model: The paper presents pytest-ranking, a Pytest plugin that implements three lightweight Regression Test Prioritization techniques: QTF, which prioritizes shorter-running tests; RecentFail, which prioritizes tests that have failed recently; and SimChgPath, which prioritizes tests whose IDs are textually similar to recently changed Python file paths. A Hybrid technique linearly combines the three normalized scores using configurable weights. The tool is also hierarchy-aware and can prioritize tests at PUT, function, module, or directory granularity.
Results: Across the 14 projects, the proposed Hybrid technique achieved the best overall mean APFDc of 0.83, compared with 0.47 for Pytest Default and 0.50 for Random. The authors report that RTP techniques were 38%–77% better than Default and 30%–66% better than Random across projects. The individual techniques achieved mean APFDc values of 0.78 (QTF), 0.65 (RecentFail), and 0.66 (SimChgPath). The Hybrid approach was therefore 77% better than Default and 66% better than Random in the overall comparison. The tool itself introduced only 0.1 seconds of average runtime overhead, equivalent to approximately 0.03% of total test-suite execution time. Its cached RTP data required 6–538 KB, or approximately 1%–9% of CI log size (5% on average). The study also found 146 flaky tests among the failed TSRs, of which 112 (77%) were order-dependent; 1,035 regression tests were identified.
Contribution: The paper contributes a practical, open-source RTP plugin for Python/Pytest rather than only proposing another research algorithm. It integrates multiple simple prioritization signals—test execution time, recent failures, and code-change relatedness—into a configurable Hybrid ranking mechanism and supports CI deployment, test selection, parallelization, and different test-suite hierarchy levels. A particularly important contribution is the realistic evaluation: instead of only simulating reordered test results on historical data, the authors actually reran historical GitHub Actions builds and observed real execution behavior, including flaky and order-dependent tests.
Limitation: The evaluation is restricted to Python projects using Pytest and GitHub Actions, so the findings cannot be directly generalized to other languages, testing frameworks, or CI systems. Although the researchers initially collected 27,224 builds, only 718 builds were selected for the six-order rerun experiment because of computational constraints. Some historical builds also could not be rerun because of stale branches, unavailable old dependencies, or other early-exit errors. The actual CI evaluation revealed that order-dependent flaky tests are common (77% of the identified flaky tests), which can complicate RTP effectiveness because changing test order can itself affect outcomes.

Dataset: The study evaluates Similo and its extensions using both three existing benchmarks and a newly constructed extended benchmark. The original Similo benchmark contains 809 web-element pairs from 48 websites, while the VON Similo benchmark contains 1,163 element pairs derived from 442 base elements across 33 websites. The LLM VON Similo benchmark contains 804 element pairs. The authors' new benchmark contains 10,376 element pairs, derived from 933 initial elements across 30 selected popular web applications, with website snapshots collected at four-month intervals from September 2018 to September 2023. The extended benchmark is approximately 12× larger than the original Similo benchmark and 23× larger than the VON Similo benchmark.
Preprocessing Method: Website versions were collected from the Wayback Machine, and the researchers reloaded the same archived snapshots used by the original studies to make comparisons consistent. They manually tracked web elements across versions and classified changes as No Change, Minor Change, or Major Change. They also categorized locator status according to whether all locators worked, Absolute XPath failed, or no basic unique locator worked. For similarity computation, DOM properties such as ID, class, name, tag, text, XPath, coordinates, dimensions, and other attributes were extracted. Different property types were compared using appropriate similarity functions such as Levenshtein, equality, Euclidean, and 2D distance, with additional functions such as Jaccard and Jaro-Winkler evaluated in the optimization process.
Model: The paper is a replication and extension study, rather than a completely new standalone model. It evaluates Similo, VON Similo, LLM VON Similo (using its benchmark but not fully replicated because its GPT-4 configuration is not reproducible), and three extensions: Similo++, VON Similo++, and HybridSimilo. Similo ranks candidate web elements according to a weighted similarity score over DOM properties. Similo++ optimizes the properties, similarity functions, and weights using a Genetic Algorithm. VON Similo uses Visually Overlapping Nodes (VONs) to capture groups of elements that form a visual unit. HybridSimilo first uses VON Similo++ to select the top 10 candidates and then applies Similo++ to identify the exact target element.
Results: The replication closely matched previous results: Similo achieved 88.99% localization compared with 88.64% in the original study, while the replicated VON Similo configuration achieved 91.65% compared with 91.29% originally. On the LLM VON Similo benchmark, optimizing Similo improved Exact Match (M4) from 87.54% to 91.78% and Visual/Textual Overlap (M3) from 91.65% to 95.64%. HybridSimilo achieved 95.51% M3 on that benchmark, slightly above the 95.0% reported for LLM VON Similo. Most importantly for broken locator recovery, the original Similo correctly identified 95.8% of elements whose original locators no longer worked, while the optimized approach reached approximately 98.8%. On the extended benchmark, HybridSimilo also achieved 98.8% localization for broken-locator elements in the reported testing scenarios. Dataset: The study does not use a real industrial dataset directly. Because the replication package of the baseline study was unavailable, the authors reverse-engineered synthetic test sets while preserving the reported aggregate execution-time budget and mean pairwise Jaccard similarity of 14.09%. They created two datasets: one with 80–248 requirements/tests and a second with 40–124, obtained by halving the input size. For the value-aware experiment, 248 requirements were assigned Fibonacci-based Business Values ranging from 2 to 89, while test execution times were sampled from an exponential distribution.

Business Value is assigned to requirements using a Fibonacci-based scale (2–89), and execution times are generated using an exponential distribution. The authors create a smaller second dataset by halving the number of requirements and tests while keeping other factors constant. A requirement is counted as covered only when all of its associated validating tests are selected, enforcing a strict requirement-level definition of done.

The two optimization objectives are (1) total Business Value of fully covered requirements and (2) percentage of requirements covered, while total execution time must remain within the Regression Test Window. NSGA-II uses tournament selection, crossover, mutation, a repair operator, non-dominated sorting, and crowding distance to produce Pareto-optimal test sets.
Results: NSGA-II consistently achieved the highest Business Value across most Regression Test Windows, with its clearest advantage occurring around 10%–40% RTW. Requirement coverage increased for all methods as the testing window increased; NSGA-II and BCPSO both exceeded 50% coverage by approximately 20% RTW, while above 75% RTW all three methods exceeded approximately 85–90% coverage and converged. NSGA-II and BCPSO had similar coverage, but NSGA-II consistently achieved higher Business Value.
Contribution: The paper reframes Regression Test Selection as a business-value preservation problem rather than optimizing only technical measures such as coverage or cost. It introduces a value-aware, time-constrained multi-objective formulation and demonstrates it using NSGA-II. Its main contribution is showing that regression testing can simultaneously consider Business Value, Requirement Coverage, and limited testing time, allowing the system to favor high-value functionality when the regression budget is tight.
Limitation: The evaluation relies on synthetic/reconstructed datasets rather than real industrial regression suites. Business Values are artificially assigned using a Fibonacci 2–89 distribution, and execution times are synthetically generated from an exponential distribution. The study also compares against a relatively narrow set of baselines (BCPSO and Random). Although ANOVA and Tukey HSD are used, the authors do not report effect sizes or multiple-comparison adjustments. Contribution: The paper introduces a unified automated web-testing approach that combines Screen Transition Graphs and LLMs for site-navigation test generation with State Graphs and LLMs for complex form-filling test generation. It also contributes a benchmark containing 2,000 synthetic forms and 133 real-world forms for evaluating automated form interaction. The approach bridges navigation testing and form testing within one workflow and automatically generates Selenium-based test cases.
Limitation: The paper does not contain a separate limitations section. However, its experimental results explicitly reveal several remaining limitations: performance decreases on dynamic forms; GPT-4o's coverage falls to only 37.12% on real-world forms; hidden and file fields show consistent failures; complex form-validation rules produce more errors; and navigation robustness remains challenging, with GPT-4o-mini receiving only 5.61/10 for robustness despite a 7.60/10 overall score. These are limitations evidenced directly by the authors' evaluation rather than assumptions added from outside the paper.

Paper Title:
Microscale search-based algorithm based on time-space transfer for
automatedtest case generation
Dataset: The study does not use a conventional ML dataset. Instead, it evaluates MISA-TST on 15 open-source benchmark programs, consisting of 9 normal-scale and 6 large-scale benchmarks. The benchmarks are drawn from the iFogSim toolkit, CoreNLP toolkit, and classical benchmark functions, with benchmark programs combined to simulate large-scale unit programs. A separate F1–F8 smart-contract test set containing known and patched re-entrancy vulnerability programs is used for adversarial testing.
Preprocessing Method: The algorithm first decomposes each test-input dimension into intervals and builds a variable-interval-path relationship matrix that records relationships between specific input intervals/values and branch directions. It then identifies a smaller Effective Decision Space (EDS) for each target path and restricts the search to these relevant subspaces instead of searching the entire decision space.
Model: The proposed MISA-TST (Microscale Search-Based Algorithm with Time-Space Transfer) extends the MISA search-based test-generation approach. It combines two strategies: Dimension Partition Strategy (DPS), which divides input dimensions into intervals and identifies relevant subspaces, and Specific Value Strategy (SVS), which records specific values associated with branch-direction changes. These strategies are combined through a variable-interval-path relationship matrix to obtain smaller EDSs and reduce redundant search.
Results: MISA-TST achieved higher path coverage or significantly fewer fitness evaluations than MISA-DPS, MISA-SVS, and MISA in 8, 6, and 6 benchmarks, respectively. In benchmark No.13, containing 27,648 paths, MISA-TST covered 61.29% (16,945 paths) compared with 16.56% (4,578) for MISA-DPS, 5.49% (1,517) for MISA-SVS, and 33.01% (9,126) for MISA. Against the broader state-of-the-art algorithms, MISA-TST achieved higher path coverage or fewer FEs in 14/15 benchmarks (93.33%); it was better than RP-DE in 15/15 (100%), and achieved higher path coverage than ABC and IGA in 15/15 (100%). Compared with ESSENT, it outperformed the method in 12/15 (80%) benchmarks. In adversarial smart-contract testing, MISA-TST achieved 100% path coverage across the F1–F8 test sets while keeping test-case executions below 1.00E+05.
Contribution: The paper introduces MISA-TST, a microscale search-based test-case generation algorithm specifically designed for large-scale unit programs. Its main contribution is the variable-interval-path relationship matrix, which allows the algorithm to identify more precise and smaller EDSs. By combining dimension partition and specific value strategies, the approach reduces unnecessary search while improving path coverage. The paper also provides a set of large-scale benchmark problems for evaluating search-based ATCG-PC algorithms.
Limitation: The evaluation relies on path coverage and fitness evaluations as its main effectiveness measures. The experimental benchmarks are sampled from iFogSim, CoreNLP, and classical functions, and large-scale programs are simulated by combining benchmark programs, which limits direct generalization to all real-world applications. Parameter combinations could not all be exhaustively tested. Most importantly, the authors identify infeasible paths as an unresolved problem because searching for such paths can waste computational resources; handling infeasible paths is therefore planned as future work.

Dataset: The paper does not use a conventional ML dataset. Preprocessing Method: No conventional data preprocessing is used. The main preparation step is obtaining a test dependency graph, either manually or using TEDD. Stile then extracts dependency-respecting warranted schedules and organizes them into a prefix tree to identify shared prefixes.

Results: Stile reduced E2E test-suite execution time by 12%–80% compared with sequential execution, with 47% average saving. At 32 cores, the average saving was 53%. Compared with Selenium Grid, Stile achieved an average 33% saving at 4 cores and 11% at 8 cores, but became slower on average at 16 and 32 cores because container-cloning overhead became more significant. Stile also reduced CPU-time compared with Grid by 29%–75%, averaging 51%, and reduced the number of executed test scripts by 47% on average compared with Grid.
Contribution: Proposes Stile, a dependency-aware approach for parallelizing E2E Web test suites. Its main technical contribution is using a prefix tree to execute common test prefixes only once, followed by Docker-based application-state cloning so that dependent branches can execute independently and in parallel. It empirically validates the approach on eight open-source web applications.
Limitation: Evaluation is based on only 8 medium-size E2E test suites, so further validation on large business-grade/industrial test suites is needed. The authors also identify implementation-efficiency concerns, possible environmental confounding factors, and limitations in predicting performance from test-suite/dependency-tree properties. Dataset: The paper does not use a conventional machine-learning dataset. The approach is evaluated on six complex open-source web applications, including applications such as Parabank and Agilefant, and is additionally applied to the top 20 real-world web applications to assess its practical bug-finding capability.

During this stage, it collects GUI screenshots, HTML content, GUI actions, XPaths, application states, state transitions, and code-coverage information. When coverage stagnates, LLM-based agents summarize this collected information into a knowledge base and infer functionalities that have not yet been covered.
Model: The proposed Temac framework uses LLM-based multi-agent collaboration. It consists of three major stages: broad exploration, knowledge-base construction, and targeted task execution. The task-execution stage separates planning from GUI action execution: a reasoning-based Planner determines how to accomplish an uncovered functionality, while a specialized Actor (implemented using UI-TARS in the reported setup) locates GUI elements and performs actions such as clicking and typing.
Results: On six complex open-source web applications, Temac achieved 12.5%–60.3% higher average code coverage than state-of-the-art approaches. In an additional evaluation on the top 20 real-world web applications, Temac revealed 445 unique failures, demonstrating its ability to discover problems beyond the controlled benchmark evaluation
Contribution: The paper introduces Temac, a hybrid automated web GUI testing approach that combines the broad exploration capability of traditional AWGT with the semantic reasoning ability of LLM-based multi-agent systems. Its key contribution is the use of information collected during initial exploration to build a knowledge base, which then guides LLM agents toward uncovered and deeper application functionalities instead of asking LLMs to explore the entire application from scratch.
Limitation: The approach still depends on the limitations of LLM-based reasoning and GUI execution, including inference cost, complex application context, and imperfect task-execution success. The controlled evaluation is based on only six complex open-source web applications, so the quantitative results cannot automatically be generalized to every type of web application. In addition, the primary effectiveness measure is code coverage, which does not by itself guarantee complete functional coverage or the detection of all important defects.
